checks.note: Supported: regex preprocessing (IPs, block IDs), layer 1 = token count, leading-token layers, digit tokens go to '*' node, similarity threshold st, maxChild=100 ('empirically set maxChild to 100'). Depth 3-4 and st 0.3-0.5 are in Table II, which I did not see as text (Fig 2 uses depth 3, Fig 3 depth 4); those ranges not confirmed.

checks.quote: most of them (9 out of 15) are unable to complete the parsing process for all 14 datasets within 12 hours.
checks.note: Supported: 14 datasets, avg 3.6M lines, 15 parsers, 9 of 15 cannot finish, parsers struggle with infrequent and parameter-intensive templates, high overall scores do not guarantee good parsing of those. 'error/fatal levels' appears as 'error-level log messages' example, not as a verbatim struggle claim. Drain FGA 0.75 -> ~0.55 not found in text (likely a figure); unconfirmed. Paper says 12 hours, not 'reasonable time' alone (Finding 5 says 'reasonable 12-hour timeframe').

checks.quote: This grouping is a lot less reliable because of changing error messages.
checks.note: Order fingerprint, stack trace, exception, message is supported; in-app frames only; AI grouping 'will never split up issues that were grouped by fingerprint'. Wrong detail: the page says the message without parameters is tried first, and the full message attribute is the final fallback, not parameter-stripped as the last resort. 'Message last' holds only in the ordering sense.

checks.quote: Frames marked non-contributing with 'ignored due to recursion' when abs_path, package, module, filename, function, lineno and colno all match the previous frame (fetch summary of code).
checks.note: Supported: module/filename(lowercased basename)/function/context_line; >120 chars context line dropped; module precedence; Ruby, PHP, JS cleanups; recursion marking. Fails: Java lambda$ functions are made non-contributing, not rewritten to <auto> (CGLIB/Javassist etc. do become <auto>). No in-app frames: !app component marked non-contributing; 'system variant used' not confirmed in this file. Conflict resolved by the docs page: 'revision hashes, and so forth, removed' from normalized filename, while newstyle.py shows no hash stripping, so the docs and code disagree.

checks.quote: slight variance in a crashed stack defeat this signature's bucketing properties; Magic Signature can often be generated for disjoint crashes from different versions; crash reports by their cause, implicated by shared stack frames.
checks.note: All three signatures and their trade-offs confirmed via fetch summary; Stack Signature collides across versions. Wording of 'topmost symbol plus small callstack hash' is paraphrase of 'top symbol plus a hash of the call stack'.

checks.quote: !analyze is roughly 100,000 lines of code implementing some 500 bucketing heuristics, with roughly one heuristic added per week.
checks.note: Confirmed from locally extracted PDF text: no ideal algorithm ('We know of no such algorithm'), labeling vs classifying and expanding vs condensing axes, L15 assert_tags, module_offset contribution 67.95%, Office 2010 row 21.6/17.7/36.8/28.1, up to 6 months of raw CAB files. Not individually verified: 'second or one-hit bucket' interpretation of the 4 percentages (row is labelled 'Combined'), 6-month minidump re-run of heuristics, kernel crash re-bucketing (kernel crash buckets discussed only in an overcondensing context).

checks.quote: We observe that FTS although simple outperforms many other DBRD approaches for most projects (all except Mozilla). REP... is the overall best performer. Thus, we suggest future research include these simpler techniques as baselines.
checks.note: Also confirmed: 'Projects with a medium to low volume of historical BRs may not benefit from deep learning-based tools'; FTS deployed by Mozilla; abstract says simpler technique outperforms sophisticated ones on most projects; related work: execution information (stack traces) beneficial 'but not many BRs contain such execution information' (attributed to Wang et al.). Minor: paper says FTS beats many approaches for most projects, except Mozilla; the summary's 'on some projects' is looser.
